**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Religious Studies 3 (0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Paper 3: The New Testament, Religion in Relation to Philosophy, Ethics and Morality, Historical Development of Islam (570CE-661CE). Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

The paper has six sections of six questions each: Section 2.1 The Gospel According to Luke (questions 1-6); Section 2.2 The Fourth Gospel (questions 7-12); Section 2.3 The Early Church as Reflected in Acts and 1 Corinthians (questions 13-18); Section 4.1 Philosophy of Religion (questions 19-24); Section 4.2 Ethics and Morality (questions 25-30); Section 6.0 The Historical Development of Islam (570CE - 661CE) (questions 31-36).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Assess which logical or evidential aspects of the problem of evil pose the greatest challenge.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The problem of evil is the challenge to belief in an all-powerful and all-good God posed by the existence of evil and suffering. Philosophers distinguish a *logical* form, which says that the belief is self-contradictory, from an *evidential* form, which says that the evil in the world is evidence against the existence of such a God. This answer assesses which of the two poses the greater challenge.

**1. The logical problem.**
- J. L. Mackie argued in 1955 that the statements "God is omnipotent", "God is wholly good" and "evil exists" form an inconsistent set, since a good God would want to remove evil and an omnipotent God could do so. To make the set inconsistent one needs extra premises, such as that a good being always eliminates evil as far as it can.
- *Responses.* Alvin Plantinga's free will defence says that it is logically possible that God could not create free beings who always choose the good, and that a world with free beings is better than one without; and God is not responsible for the evil freely chosen. Many philosophers, including some who are not believers, now accept that this shows that there is no logical contradiction. Other responses are Augustine's view of evil as a privation of good, and the point that omnipotence does not include doing the logically impossible.
- *Remaining challenge.* The free will defence does not explain *natural evil* (earthquakes, disease, disasters such as the 1986 Lake Nyos gas disaster in Cameroon), unless it is linked to the actions of spiritual beings or to the laws of nature needed for a stable world.

**2. The evidential problem.**
- The evidential argument does not claim a contradiction but says that the amount, kind and distribution of evil make the existence of God unlikely. William Rowe argued that some evils appear to be *gratuitous*: they serve no greater good that even an omnipotent God could not have achieved otherwise, as in the case of the suffering of a fawn burned in a forest fire, or the prolonged suffering of innocent children.
- David Hume had earlier pointed to the waste and cruelty of nature as evidence against a benevolent designer.
- *Responses.* John Hick's soul-making theodicy says that a world with challenges is needed for moral and spiritual growth toward a final good beyond death; the Augustinian approach links evil to the Fall and sees the final justice of God; process thinkers modify the idea of omnipotence. Sceptical theism holds that human beings cannot expect to know God's reasons, so the appearance of gratuitous evil does not count against God. Christians often point to the suffering of God in Christ on the cross.
- *Remaining challenge.* Each response has difficulties: critics say that the amount of suffering is too great and too unfairly distributed for soul-making, that the Fall is not credible in the light of science, that the sceptical response makes belief difficult to test, and that heaven does not undo past suffering.

**3. Assessment.** The logical problem is the more severe on paper, since if it succeeded it would disprove God outright; but it is widely regarded as answered, because the premise needed to make a contradiction cannot be shown to be necessary. The evidential problem remains more serious today because it deals with the actual world and with probabilities, and it is harder to answer decisively, especially with regard to natural evil and the suffering of the innocent. It also touches ordinary people, who experience pain, in a way that technical logic does not.

**Conclusion.** The greater challenge comes from the evidential aspects, particularly gratuitous and natural evil, since the logical problem has been largely answered by the free will defence. However, believers may argue that the evidence is not decisive, and faith and revelation provide reasons to trust God even without a full explanation.
